transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2027-02-17 16:00 UTC
Duration: ~68 minutes
Attendees: Priya Rao (Redwood AE), Diego Morales (Redwood SE), Anya Patel (Redwood SRE); Ravi Menon (Mistral Foundry), Janelle Kaur (ML Infra), Omar N'diaye (Security), Sofia Li (Backend)

Summary (auto): deep dive on KV cache residency and eviction; customer on-prem constraints; action items captured.

[00:00] Priya Rao: Hey everybody, thanks for joining. quick intro: i'm Priya, i'll run the session and Diego's going to drive the runtime traces and tests. we planned to walk through their long-context failure patterns and map them to the KV "thermostat" settings we talked about.

[00:22] Ravi Menon: thanks Priya. to set context, we run multi-turn agents with 60k-120k token histories, heavy prefix reuse across many sessions. we're seeing periodic latency spikes and session dropouts when our on-prem cluster is under burst.

[00:40] Diego Morales: got it. when you say prefix reuse, do you mean many sessions sharing the same system prompt plus small user variations? or do you have many distinct prefixes?

[00:52] Janelle Kaur: yep, same system prompt across teams, but varying user context appended. so hot prefixes are pretty concentrated. we also snapshot KV in a way that sometimes leads to overlap between sessions.

[01:10] Diego: that aligns with hotset behavior. quick note: Redwood runtime has a thermostat-like controller that balances KV residency using access frequency, recency, and a memory-watermark. if the hotset is extremely heavy the eviction policies start paging to disk / spillback.

[01:35] Omar N'diaye: can you clarify "paging" in our on-prem env — is that local SSD, network NFS, or a Redwood-managed spill tier? For compliance we need data to never leave our VPC unencrypted.

[01:50] Priya: great question. for hosted we have a managed spill tier but for Private/on-prem we support configurable spill policies: local NVMe or encrypted NFS inside the customer's VPC. defaults are encrypted at rest; KMS integration is supported. we'll share the config doc.

[02:12] Diego: demoing a trace now — i'll share my screen (link: benchmark-spreadsheet.xlsx). this trace shows a 45s window where repeated long-context requests triggered a large prefix reconstruction and the runtime started evicting older KV segments. you'll see prefix collisions and ordering jitter.

[02:35] [Diego screen share, garbled auto-caption: "three hundred or 3.0..."]

[03:00] Sofia Li: what do you mean by "prefix collision" — is that two different sessions referencing the same kv key id?

[03:08] Diego: yes, exactly. our KV uses a prefix hash to co-locate keys; when many sessions map to a small set of prefixes, you get hotspots. hot prefixes lead to cache thrash because the runtime tries to keep most-recent chunks but eviction has to pick between many active contexts.

[03:40] Janelle: we also noticed that quantized models seem to change page residency — smaller footprint but more frequent cache churn. any insight?

[03:55] Anya Patel: quantization reduces model memory but can increase working set fragmentation since kernels access different alignment sizes; combined with prefix reuse that can increase eviction pressure. we saw similar effects in staging.

[04:18] Diego: exactly. also batch sizing plays into this: large batches improve throughput but they lock more KV ranges for the duration of request processing, increasing effective residency. small routed requests lower contention but can increase per-token compute cost. it's a latency vs cost tradeoff.

[04:45] Ravi: our primary SLA is P95 < 600ms for interactive assistants. can your runtime meet that with this long-context profile?

[04:55] Priya: yes, with two caveats — either we adapt the thermostat thresholds to favor low-latency residency for pinned prefixes, or you provision dedicated capacity with larger GPU memory and tuned batching. the latter reduces cost predictability but gives deterministic latency.

[05:20] Omar: from a security standpoint, if we go Dedicated or Private, we need: SSO + SAML, KMS/HSM integration, audit logs salted for token IDs, and the ability to restrict spill to NVMe inside our subnet. does Redwood support all of that?

[05:35] Priya: yes. we support SAML SSO, KMS integrations (AWS KMS, Azure Key Vault), and can restrict spill mounting to customer-managed volumes. we'll drop the SOC2 + architecture docs.

[05:55] Diego: jumping back: here's a pathological timeline (timestamps in trace). you'll see at [00:12:25] the KV controller bumped memory-watermark, started incremental eviction; at [00:12:42] there was an interleaved batch which required rehydrating a prefix from disk which led to a 1.8s token stall.

[06:30] Sophia (auto-caption mistake): "one point eight seconds" is typed as "1.8lbs" — ignore caption.

[06:45] Janelle: is there a way to prioritize specific prefixes to be pinned? some of our system prompts are business-critical.

[06:55] Diego: yes, you can pin prefixes at deployment time and set tenant-level pin budgets; pinned keys never evict unless you explicitly unpin. but pinning increases memory usage; thermostat will then evict non-pinned ranges more aggressively.

[07:20] Ravi: we tried pinning but still hit spill during burst windows — maybe the pinned budget wasn't high enough. what heuristics do you use to recommend pin budgets?

[07:35] Anya: we recommend starting with a heatmap-based approach: sample production traffic for 24-72 hours, compute per-prefix access percentiles, and set pin budget to cover the 95th-percentile hotset size. Diego will provide a script for that.

[07:58] Diego: yes, i'll share the sampling script and a heatmap exporter (link: /redwood/tools/kv-heatmap).

[08:12] Sofia: can we do runtime autoscaling of pin budgets per burst? i.e., temporarily bump pinned capacity during a predictable daily peak?

[08:22] Diego: there is a feature called "pin surge" where you can temporarily raise the pin budget with a TTL; it's helpful but must be used carefully to avoid thrashing when the surge ends. we typically combine it with prefetch warmups so rehydration cost is amortized.

[08:45] Janelle: prefetch warmups — is that proactive loading of likely keys into KV before traffic arrives?

[08:52] Diego: yes. warmup heuristics can be static (scheduled) or dynamic (model-driven prediction). for Mistral Foundry's workload we suggested a hybrid: scheduled warmup for daily batch jobs + dynamic prefetch for session starters identified by event hooks.

[09:12] Ravi: about paging thresholds — how do you choose between local NVMe spill vs remote spill? local NVMe is faster but more expensive; remote spill gives you more capacity.

[09:24] Priya: recommend local NVMe for latency-sensitive prefixes; remote blobstore is for cost-optimized archival spill. on Private deployments you control that tradeoff — Redwood's default is local encrypted NVMe if available.

[09:40] Omar: one more security question — when KV spills to disk, is the content tokenized or stored as raw token ids? What are the protections against token leakage?

[09:52] Anya: internal format is compressed token ids + prefix metadata; we support field-level encryption for certain sensitive prefixes and KMS-wrapped keys per tenant. audit logs include spill events and checksums.

[10:10] Diego: switching to batching: We observed that batch length correlation with eviction increases non-linearly. At small batch sizes (<4 requests) eviction pressure is low; at medium batch sizes (4-16) throughput improves but you see lock contention; above 16 it tends to spike KV residency and stall rehydrations.

[10:36] Janelle: interesting. our traffic is a mix — 80% single-user routed calls, 20% batched background generation. so maybe tune two separate runtime pools?

[10:47] Diego: yes, segregating pools by workload class is effective: low-latency pool with small batch sizes and high memory per GPU; throughput pool with larger batches and quantized models. routing policies can direct requests based on headers.

[11:05] Ravi: how hard is it to run two pools in Private/on-prem?

[11:10] Priya: it's supported; you run multiple node pools and set routing rules in the control plane. for on-prem that means coordinating with your infra team for node labels and NIC VLANs — Diego and Anya can share a runbook.

[11:25] Diego: here's a failed run example — note the waveform at [00:22:10] where multiple sessions touched the same prefix and the runtime issued concurrent rehydration reads; this saturated the IO path and caused backpressure leading to request timeouts.

[11:48] Sofia: is there read-side backpressure mitigation? can you multiplex rehydration reads or queue them?

[11:54] Diego: we have an IO throttler that serializes rehydration for the same prefix and rate-limits parallel reads to the same NVMe. it helps but at very high QPS you still need either more IO bandwidth or fewer concurrent rehydrations (prefetch helps).

[12:20] Omar: for audit we need visibility into rehydration events — can logs be forwarded to our SIEM with fielded metadata?

[12:28] Anya: yes, we can ship structured logs (JSON) of rehydration events, including prefix id, timestamp, node id, and correlation id. we'll provide an integration example for Splunk/Datadog.

[12:45] Diego: switching gears — quantization interplay: using 4-bit quantized weights freed GPU memory but increased model kernel fragmentation, causing weird access patterns in KV usage. we saw more frequent small KV reads instead of fewer large reads, which increases IO transactions and latency variance.

[13:10] Janelle: would you recommend not quantizing for latency-sensitive pool?

[13:16] Priya: right — quantization is great for throughput pool; for your interactive SLA consider slightly higher precision or mixed-precision profiles. Optimize kernels for sequence lengths in your long-context distribution; Diego can propose a profile.

[13:30] Diego: action: i'll run two micro-benchmarks: (A) quantized vs FP16 residency patterns; (B) batch-size sweep with pinned vs unpinned prefixes. will post results.

[13:42] Ravi: we also have intermittent prefix-ID collisions due to a legacy keying scheme. sometimes two logical prefixes map to the same hash shard — can that be remapped without downtime?

[13:55] Diego: yes, you can remap shards using a rolling migration: mark old prefixes as alias, warm new prefix location, switch routing with a brief overlap window. it's doable with zero downtime if carefully orchestrated. we'll share the migration playbook.

[14:15] Sofia: what's the recommended observability set for us to track?

[14:22] Anya: baseline metrics: KV hit-rate by prefix, eviction rate, memory-watermark, IO latency P50/P95, rehydration count, batch lock time, GPU memory pressure, and per-request trace IDs. Diego will add example dashboards.

[14:40] Priya: quick note on cost: Dedicated capacity pricing will look different if you pin a large hotset; we can model cost per 1k requests given your heatmap once you provide telemetry.

[14:55] Ravi: can we run a 1-hour production-sim test in your sandbox with our long-context set? we'd like to see the real-world behavior.

[15:05] Priya: yes, Diego will provision a mimic cluster in Redwood's private staging for that run — we just need your prompt set and a small allowlist for data handling.

[15:18] Diego: noting: need long-context prompts, expected session concurrency pattern, and your on-prem IO profile.

[15:28] Janelle: we'll provide that by Monday.

[15:35] Omar: and we'll need to review the KMS key policies before any spill testing.

[15:42] Priya: understood. we'll send the security pack and the KMS sample policy.

[15:55] Diego: last technical note — fallback strategies. when KV is under pressure, runtime can fall back to a degraded mode: shorter context window, approximate prefix matching, or model-level short-circuit to smaller context. this keeps availability but may reduce response quality. choose per-route fallback policies.

[16:20] Ravi: that's promising. we'll want to tune fallbacks conservatively.

[16:30] Priya: summary of decisions: run 1-hour stress test in Redwood staging, share heatmap scripts and docs, share security pack and runbook for on-prem migration, Diego to run microbenchmarks, customer to share prompts and concurrency profile.

[16:50] Janelle: thanks, this was super helpful.

[16:55] Priya: thanks everyone. i'll follow up with notes and links.

[17:00] call end
